title: Reporting a School Energy Audit
description: Edit a full informational passage for grammar, punctuation, usage, and clarity.
subject: rla
passage:
Students in an environmental science class completed a month-long energy audit of their school building. The project was not designed to produce a complete engineering study. Instead, the class wanted to identify simple patterns that could guide future questions about electricity use.

Teams recorded whether classroom lights and projectors were left on during lunch, after classes, and during several weekend activities. They also reviewed monthly electricity bills from the previous year. The students found that unnecessary lighting was common in a few hallways and shared rooms, but the billing records did not allow them to determine exactly how much electricity those lights used by themselves.

The class prepared a short report for the school administration. The report recommends clearer shutdown reminders and a two-month trial in which selected rooms are checked at the end of each day. Students suggest comparing those observations with the same period from the previous year, while also recording major schedule changes that might affect electricity use.

The teacher reminded students not to claim that the audit proved a particular cause of the school’s total energy use. Weather, air-conditioning demand, weekend events, and equipment changes can all influence the monthly bill. The report therefore separates what students directly observed from what they still need to test. Before publication, the class is editing the report for concise wording, clear pronoun references, correct capitalization, and punctuation that helps readers follow the limits of the evidence.

The students are also revising a table that lists their observations by location and time of day. The table will appear beside a short explanation of what the observations can and cannot show. For example, seeing lights on in an empty room confirms that electricity was being used at that moment, but it does not reveal the room's total share of the monthly bill. The class wants the wording around the table to preserve that distinction.

During peer review, students will underline every sentence that states a conclusion and circle the evidence used to support it. If a conclusion sounds more certain than the evidence allows, they will revise the wording before checking grammar and punctuation. The final editing pass will then focus on sentence boundaries, possessives, transitions, and unnecessary phrases so that language errors do not make the report's cautious reasoning harder to follow.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct capitalization. Here 'environmental science' names the subject generally, not an official course title.
questions.explanation: The generic subject name is lowercase; the month 'March' is capitalized.
questions.rule: Capitalize proper names and calendar names, not ordinary school subjects used generically.

options.text: The Environmental Science class reviewed bills from March.
options.whyWrong: A school subject used generically is usually lowercase unless it is a language or part of a formal course title.

options.text: The environmental science class reviewed bills from march.
The environmental science class reviewed bills from March.
The Environmental science class reviewed bills from March.
options.whyWrong: The generic subject phrase should not be partly capitalized.

questions.prompt: Choose the clearest pronoun revision: “The class compared the bills with the schedule because it had changed.”
questions.explanation: The revision names the changed item, 'schedule,' and keeps the later pronoun reference clear.
questions.rule: When a pronoun could point to multiple nouns, name the intended noun.

options.text: The class compared the bills with the schedule because it had changed.
options.whyWrong: 'It' could refer to the class, bill set, or schedule.

options.text: The class compared them with it because it changed.
options.whyWrong: The pronouns do not identify the intended nouns clearly.

options.text: It changed, so it compared the bills with the schedule.
options.whyWrong: Both instances of 'it' lack a clear antecedent.

options.text: Because the schedule had changed, the class compared it with the bills.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct possessive: “The {{blank}} report separates observations from conclusions.”
questions.explanation: The report belongs to multiple students, so the plural possessive is students'.
questions.rule: For a regular plural ending in s, add only an apostrophe.

options.text: student's
options.whyWrong: This shows possession by one student rather than the group.

options.text: students'
students
options.whyWrong: The plural noun does not show possession of the report.

options.text: students's
options.whyWrong: A regular plural ending in s takes only an apostrophe for possession.

questions.prompt: Choose the most concise revision: “The report makes a recommendation that the school should conduct a two-month trial.”
questions.explanation: The direct verb 'recommends' preserves the meaning in far fewer words.
questions.rule: Prefer strong direct verbs over noun-heavy phrases when no nuance is lost.

options.text: The report recommends a two-month trial.
The report makes a recommendation that the school should conduct a two-month trial.
options.whyWrong: 'Makes a recommendation that' can be replaced by the direct verb 'recommends'.

options.text: The report gives a recommendation in regard to the conducting of a two-month trial.
options.whyWrong: This turns a direct action into several abstract noun phrases.

options.text: A recommendation is made by the report for the purpose of a two-month trial.
options.whyWrong: The passive wording is longer and less direct.

questions.prompt: The class observed lights left on; {{blank}}, the billing records cannot show how much those lights alone cost.
questions.explanation: 'However' introduces the important limitation on what the observation can establish.
questions.rule: Use contrast transitions to signal a limit, exception, or difference.

options.text: therefore
options.whyWrong: The limitation is not a result proving a cost figure.

options.text: for example
options.whyWrong: The billing limitation is not an example of observing lights left on.

options.text: however
similarly
options.whyWrong: The two statements have different roles; the second limits the first.

questions.explanation: The complete clause introduces a list, so the colon is appropriate.
questions.rule: Place a colon after a complete statement, not between a verb and its object.

options.text: Several factors can affect: the bill, weather, events, and equipment changes.
options.whyWrong: The colon incorrectly interrupts the verb and its object.

options.text: Several factors can affect the bill; weather, events, and equipment changes.
options.whyWrong: A semicolon does not introduce a simple list fragment.

options.text: Several factors can affect the bill, weather, events, and equipment changes.
options.whyWrong: The comma does not clearly signal that the following items are examples of the factors.

options.text: Several factors can affect the bill: weather, events, and equipment changes.
